papers.title: Managing Dissociation and Somatic Symptoms in Complex PTSD Using a Structural Dissociation-informed Approach: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Chronic interpersonal trauma can lead to complex clinical presentations characterized by dissociation, somatic symptoms, and disturbances in self-organization, particularly when psychosocial stressors remain active. This case report describes a 32-year-old female with prolonged interpersonal trauma who presented with dissociative episodes, somatic symptoms including fainting and jaw locking, recurrent suicidal ideation, and significant functional impairment. Symptoms intensified amid ongoing interpersonal conflict and financial stress. Assessment findings supported a diagnosis of complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) with prominent dissociative and somatic features. Treatment followed a phase-oriented approach informed by the structural dissociation model developed by Onno van der Hart, Ellert Nijenhuis, and Kathy Steele. Intervention progressed through stabilization, trauma-focused work, and integration, incorporating psychoeducation, grounding, body-based interventions, affect regulation, and bottom-up approaches including titration and pendulation. Over the course of therapy, improvements were observed in awareness of dissociative experiences, emotional regulation, sleep, and daily functioning. Anxiety, depressive, and dissociative symptoms showed partial reduction, and suicidal behaviors decreased, although suicidal ideation remained intermittently present. Somatic dissociative symptoms, including fainting episodes, persisted but became more predictable and manageable. Given the concurrent psychotropic medication and single-case design, these changes cannot be attributed to psychotherapy alone. This case illustrates the application of a phase-oriented, structural dissociation-informed approach in CPTSD with prominent dissociative and somatic symptoms, while highlighting the challenges of treatment amid ongoing psychosocial adversity.

papers.title: Multidimensional sleep characteristics and arterial stiffness in older adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a multidimensional behavior encompassing duration, quality, and behavioral patterns. The associations between sleep characteristics and arterial stiffness remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the associations between multidimensional sleep characteristics and arterial stiffness in older adults. This cross-sectional study included 243 community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years. Arterial stiffness was assessed using the cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI). Sleep parameters-including time in bed (TIB), sleep duration, sleep latency, sleep restfulness score (SRS), daytime sleepiness, and nocturia-were evaluated using standardized self-administered questionnaires. Multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to assess independent associations between sleep characteristics and CAVI after adjustment for potential confounders. The mean age was 76.4 years, and the mean CAVI was 8.90 ± 1.03. CAVI differed significantly across TIB, SRS, and nocturia categories, with higher values observed in participants with prolonged TIB (≥8 h), poorer sleep restfulness, and more frequent nocturia. In contrast, sleep duration, sleep latency, and daytime sleepiness were not associated with CAVI. Poorer sleep restfulness was associated with higher arterial stiffness, although this finding was sensitive to participants with very poor sleep restfulness. Nocturia was positively associated with CAVI in unadjusted and partially adjusted analyses, but the association was attenuated after full adjustment. In older adults, poorer sleep restfulness and nocturia were associated with arterial stiffness, although these associations warrant cautious interpretation as an exploratory finding. CAVI also differed according to TIB category. These findings may provide additional information regarding vascular health.

papers.title: Protective role of high-intensity exercise and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced alterations in hippocampal gene expression and spatial learning.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function by disrupting hippocampal signaling pathways essential for memory formation. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and lactate, a metabolic byproduct of exercise, have demonstrated potential benefits for brain plasticity, but their protective roles during sleep deprivation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of six weeks of HIIT and lactate administration on memory-related gene expression and spatial learning in sleep-deprived rats. Forty-two male Wistar rats were divided into six groups: Control, Sleep Deprivation (SD), HIIT, HIIT + SD, Lactate, and Lactate + SD. After interventions, sleep deprivation was induced for 48 h. Spatial learning was assessed via the Morris Water Maze test, and hippocampal gene expression of PKA, LIMK, and cofilin was analyzed. The results showed no significant differences in spatial learning performance across groups; however, sleep deprivation caused significant downregulation of key genes involved in memory signaling. Both HIIT and lactate treatments effectively reversed these molecular impairments, notably increasing LIMK expression. These findings highlight the molecular protective effects of HIIT and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction and suggest their potential as non-pharmacological strategies to preserve memory function under sleep loss conditions.

papers.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of appetite and energy balance in metabolic disorders.
papers.abstract: The physiological control mechanisms that govern appetite and energy balance function through neuroendocrine systems that link central nervous system functions to peripheral organ activities and hormonal distribution pathways. The hypothalamus operates as the main control center, which processes metabolic information from hormones like leptin, insulin, ghrelin, and gut-derived peptides to govern both eating and energy use. People consume food through homeostatic processes, which control appetite together with non-homeostatic processes, which include reward pathways and circadian rhythms. The body develops metabolic disorders like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cachexia because these systems experience dysregulation. Central-peripheral communication breakdowns occur because of chronic energy surplus and inflammation, together with hormonal resistance. People establish their feeding behavior patterns through reward-related dopaminergic signaling, circadian misalignment, and sex hormone fluctuations. Researchers have discovered that neuroinflammation, genetic, epigenetic factors, and newly identified neuropeptides all contribute to the metabolic diseases that they study. Therapeutic strategies that target neuroendocrine pathways, which include GLP-1 receptor agonists, melanocortin receptor agonists, and bariatric surgery, demonstrate potential to restore appetite control and enhance metabolic health. This study explains how neuroendocrine systems control appetite and how metabolic disorders disrupt these regulatory processes while identifying new therapeutic possibilities and future research needs in metabolic neuroscience.

papers.title: Shift work and hormonal-circadian disruption raise urinary incontinence: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) is a multifactorial condition that affects a large proportion of women, compromising urogenital support and producing symptoms such as urinary incontinence (UI). The structural and functional integrity of the pelvic floor depends on coordinated interactions among muscular, hormonal, and neuroendocrine systems. Evidence indicates that circadian misalignment, particularly in women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and endocrine disruption, can influence pelvic floor physiology through melatonin suppression, cortisol dysregulation, and inflammatory activation. This review intends to synthesize current evidence on the links between circadian rhythm disruption, hormonal imbalance, and PFD, with specific emphasis on occupational shift work as a model of chronic chronobiological stress, highlighting their integrated pathophysiological mechanisms and preventive approaches. We conducted a narrative literature review using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science covering the period from January 2020 to October 2025. Studies investigating the relationship between circadian regulation, hormonal modulation, and pelvic floor function were included. Particular attention was given to research addressing melatonin and cortisol pathways, estrogen modulation, and occupational factors such as night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and physical overload. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials, observational studies (cross-sectional and cohort studies), translational and experimental research, and high-quality mechanistic reviews, defined by methodological rigor, comprehensive literature synthesis, and critical appraisal of evidence. Circadian rhythm disruption-characterized by decreased melatonin secretion, altered cortisol levels, and increased oxidative stress-has been associated with inflammation, impaired muscle contractility, and delayed pelvic floor tissue repair. Beyond anatomical alterations, UI is increasingly recognized as a neuroimmunoendocrine disorder in which hormonal dysregulation contributes to tissue instability and loss of urethral support. Women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, or occupational overload show higher rates of involuntary urine loss, partly mediated by endocrine desynchronization and maladaptive voiding behaviors during chronically misaligned biological rhythms. Preventive measures include supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, optimization of sleep hygiene, correction of work schedules, and local estrogen therapy when indicated. Chronobiological and immunomodulatory interventions have recently emerged as promising adjunctive strategies. Management of UI should move beyond a purely mechanical perspective toward an integrated model encompassing hormonal, metabolic, and behavioral modulation. Understanding the interactions among circadian rhythms, endocrine control, and pelvic tissue physiology may open innovative avenues for prevention and treatment, promoting precision-based, holistic care in women's health.

papers.title: Energy drinks consumption and sleeping quality of students' universities of the Chiclayo province, Peru.
papers.abstract: This study aligns with Sustainable Development Goal 3, Good Health and Well-being, which seeks to promote mental health and reduce premature mortality from non-communicable diseases. The research focuses on stimulant consumption, particularly energy drinks, as a significant risk factor affecting sleep quality among university students. In the local academic context, consuming these beverages has become a widespread and normalized practice. The study aims to address this issue by fostering healthy habits and promoting informed, responsible consumption within the university community. Accordingly, the primary objective is to determine the relationship between energy drink consumption and sleep quality among university students in Chiclayo in 2025. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was employed. The population consisted of 12,100 university students in Chiclayo, with a probabilistic sample of 373 participants. Data were collected using two Likert-scale questionnaires, validated by experts and tested for internal reliability. Findings indicate that energy drink consumption is prevalent among the student population, with most reporting moderate to high intake. Sleep quality was generally acceptable but not optimal, with many participants exhibiting medium to low sleep quality levels. Correlation analyses revealed a strong, negative, inverse relationship between energy drink consumption and sleep quality. Specifically, both the frequency of consumption and the reasons for intake were strongly associated with impaired sleep. Immediate perceived effects after consumption also correlated inversely with restorative sleep, suggesting that short-term energy gains compromise subsequent rest. The study confirms a strong negative relationship between energy drink consumption and sleep quality among university students in Chiclayo. These findings highlight that stimulant intake constitutes a significant risk factor that undermines restorative sleep, emphasizing the need for interventions promoting healthier consumption habits and improved well-being in the academic community.

papers.title: Pediatric Headache: A Practical Approach to Clinical Diagnosis and Management.
papers.abstract: Headache is among the most common neurological complaints of childhood and adolescence and can substantially impair school attendance and quality of life. A practical approach to the child with headache rests on four tasks: recognizing the primary headache phenotype, screening for the minority of children whose headache is secondary to another disorder, assessing how much the headache is disabling the child, and matching treatment intensity to that disability. Migraine and tension-type headache account for most primary headache presentations, but the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias and, rarely, painful cranial neuropathies must also be recognized because their management differs fundamentally from that of migraine. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a structured history, assessment of disability, and a careful general and neurological examination; red flags should prompt reassessment and risk stratification rather than reflexive neuroimaging, and in a child with a typical primary headache phenotype and a normal examination, routine imaging, laboratory testing, or electroencephalography is generally unnecessary. Management is multimodal: education and lifestyle measures form the foundation of care; acute treatment uses evidence-based, age-appropriate analgesics and triptans; and preventive treatment is reserved for children with substantial headache-related disability, bearing in mind the unusually high placebo response documented in pediatric migraine prevention trials. Several calcitonin gene-related peptide-targeted and device-based therapies have emerged for pediatric migraine since 2024, though pediatric evidence and regulatory status vary substantially by therapy. Tension-type headache and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias require separate diagnostic and therapeutic consideration, and treatment of the latter reflects evidence largely extrapolated from adults and case series, rather than controlled pediatric trials. This review provides a practical, evidence-based framework for the clinical diagnosis and management of pediatric headache for the general clinician.

papers.title: An Exploratory Retrospective Comparison of Crisugabalin and Pregabalin Among 12-Week Treatment Completers With Postherpetic Neuralgia.
papers.abstract: Pregabalin (PGB) is commonly used for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), but its clinical effectiveness may be limited by insufficient pain relief or adverse events (AEs). Crisugabalin (CGB) is a novel α2δ-1 ligand that has demonstrated efficacy in randomized placebo-controlled trials. However, comparative real-world evidence for CGB and PGB remains limited. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients with PHN who completed at least 12 weeks of CGB or PGB monotherapy between January and June 2025. In October 2025, a single structured telephone interview was conducted to retrospectively assess patients' recalled status at treatment initiation (T0) and at Weeks 1, 4, and 12. Outcomes included the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the physical and mental component summary scores of the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). Linear mixed effects models (LMMs) were designated as the primary analyses and adjusted for age, sex, pain location, pre-enrollment pain duration, hypertension, and diabetes. Repeated measures analysis of variance and the LMM analysis based on inverse probability weighting of propensity scores were performed as sensitivity analysis. Safety outcomes were descriptively assessed among treatment completers. A total of 113 patients were included, including 56 in the CGB group and 57 in the PGB group. In the adjusted LMMs, significant treatment-by-time interactions were observed for NRS scores (p < 0.001), PSQI scores (p < 0.001), and SF-36 mental component summary scores (p = 0.003), the extent to which these three scores of the CGB group improved over time may be higher than that of the PGB group. The treatment-by-time interactions were not statistically significant for SF-36 physical component summary scores (p = 0.377). Sensitivity analyses using repeated measures analysis of variance produced concordant findings for NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores but not for SF-36 physical component scores. At least one AE was reported by 11 of 56 patients in the CGB group and 18 of 57 patients in the PGB group, but there was no overall significant difference in AEs (p = 0.196). Among patients who completed 12 weeks of treatment, the CGB group was associated with statistical differences to some extent in NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores than PGB group, and these degree of improvement over time may be more pronounced. Due to the substantial bias in retrospective studies and the relatively small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory, merely have reference value, and require more confirmation in prospective controlled studies in the future.

papers.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Multiple Sclerosis: A Topical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) are a relatively new class of drugs that were initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and, subsequently, weight reduction in patients with obesity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is commonly associated with comorbidities for which GLP-1RAs are indicated. An increasing prevalence of comorbid chronic diseases has increased the number of people living with MS (pwMS) who are prescribed a GLP-1RA, for indications of obesity, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, and/or chronic kidney disease. This review addresses the following key considerations: (1) the use of GLP-1RAs for weight loss in pwMS and obesity, including considerations related to drug tolerability and safety; (2) the efficacy of the GLP-1RAs for their approved non-MS indications in pwMS; and (3) the potentially pleiotropic effects of the GLP-1RAs on the MS disease course beyond their approved indications.
papers.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

papers.title: How do Uncompensated Micro-Shifts Systematically Confound Low-Concentration Metabolite Quantification in 1H-MRS Analysis?
papers.abstract: Linear combination model fitting is widely used for spectral analysis in 1H-MRS but relies on basis sets with fixed spin-system parameters, implicitly neglecting the sensitivity of chemical shifts to physiological and pathological tissue microenvironments. This study systematically evaluated the impact of frequency perturbations on spectral analysis and reassessed the validity of the Cramér-Rao lower bounds (CRLB) as a quality-control metric for low-concentration metabolites. The effects of frequency perturbations on spectral analysis were investigated using simulated datasets with different baseline models and lineshapes, followed by validation in a publicly available in vivo human brain 1H-MRS dataset (n = 31). Estimated metabolite concentrations, relative concentration changes, estimation errors, and CRLB values were analyzed across all conditions. Frequency perturbations produced minimal quantification changes in high-concentration metabolites but substantially larger errors in several low-concentration metabolites. Across both simulations and in vivo validation, relative concentration changes generally remained below 3% for high-concentration metabolites but exceeded 10%-20% for several low-concentration metabolites, including Gln, GSH, Asp, and NAAG. Importantly, substantial estimation errors frequently occurred despite CRLB values remaining within conventionally acceptable ranges. These findings were consistently observed across different baseline models, lineshapes, and in vivo validation. Physiologically relevant frequency perturbations can introduce substantial quantification bias that is not consistently reflected by CRLB. These findings identify environmentally induced resonance-frequency variations as an underrecognized source of quantification error in current linear-combination model fitting and suggest that CRLB alone is insufficient for assessing quantification reliability, particularly under conditions associated with altered brain temperature or tissue pH.

papers.title: Evaluation of the brachial plexus and spinal cord with diffusion tensor imaging and synthetic MRI in obstetric brachial plexus palsy: DTI of brachial plexus and spinal cord in OBPP.
papers.abstract: Obstetric brachial plexus palsy (OBPP) is conventionally staged as a peripheral nerve injury, yet conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) poorly reflects microstructural neural and spinal cord changes. We evaluate whether magnetic resonance image compilation (MAGIC), a form of synthetic MRI, shows strong agreement with conventional T2-weighted short-tau inversion recovery (T2-STIR) for postganglionic injury detection, compare diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics between injured and adjacent intact segments of the brachial plexus and spinal cord, and explore whether these metrics predict recovery at 2-year follow-up in infants with OBPP. In this single-center cohort with prospective enrollment and ambispective outcome assessment, 40 infants (aged 3-30 weeks) with unilateral OBPP underwent 3-T MRI during physiological sleep, comprising conventional T2-STIR, synthetic MRI (MAGIC T2-STIR), and DTI. Two blinded neuroradiologists compared synthetic and conventional sequences for postganglionic lesion detection (weighted κ). The DTI-derived fractional anisotropy (FA) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) were measured at the neural foramen (dorsal root ganglion level) and spinal cord at every injured segment and at the nearest intact segments above and below; per infant, the minimum injured value and the mean intact value were compared and related to Narakas type and 2-year recovery. Synthetic MRI showed strong agreement with conventional T2-STIR (κ = 0.84-1.00); the intraobserver repeatability of DTI measurements was good to excellent [intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.842-0.999), except for intact spinal cord ADC (ICC = 0.662). Compared with intact reference segments, injured segments showed lower FA and higher ADC at both the neural foramen (FA = 0.236 ± 0.092 vs. 0.433 ± 0.130; ADC = 2,116 ×10-6 vs. 1,191.25 ×10-6 mm2/s) and the spinal cord (FA = 0.321 ± 0.107 vs. 0.448 ± 0.143; ADC = 2,253.5 ×10-6 vs. 1,191 ×10-6 mm2/s) (all P < 0.001). Neither FA nor ADC differed by Narakas type or predicted 2-year recovery. Synthetic MRI showed strong agreement with conventional T2-STIR for the detection of postganglionic OBPP and provided six contrasts from a single acquisition of similar duration; DTI abnormalities at injured segments extended to the spinal cord, suggesting that microstructural change in OBPP may not be confined to the peripheral nerve. Segmental DTI abnormality within the spinal cord raises the possibility that OBPP injury extends centrally; confirmation would require higher-resolution acquisition, technical validation against partial-volume and cerebrospinal fluid effects, and larger longitudinal cohorts before any implication for injury classification.

papers.title: Event-Weighted Desaturation Burden and Cardiovascular Mortality in Sleep Apnoea: Findings from a Large Community-Based Prospective Cohort.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea's prognostic value is limited by reliance on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), which fails to capture physiological heterogeneity of respiratory events. We developed a composite metric, event-weighted desaturation burden (EWDB), integrating weighted respiratory event load, regularity of consecutive inter-event intervals, and cumulative desaturation area. We evaluated its association with cardiovascular mortality and its incremental prognostic value compared with AHI and established hypoxic metrics. We analysed 4,904 adults from the Sleep Heart Health Study with baseline polysomnography and adjudicated follow-up. EWDB was derived by combining a respiratory weighted index, a distribution factor based on inter-event interval regularity, and event-linked hypoxic burden (HB). The primary outcome was cardiovascular mortality. Over a median follow-up of approximately 11 years, 341 cardiovascular deaths occurred. In fully adjusted multivariable Cox models, higher EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality. However, AHI and HB associations were attenuated and lost statistical significance after full adjustment. EWDB (per 1-SD increase) remained robustly associated with cardiovascular mortality, whereas AHI did not. Incorporating EWDB into a comprehensive clinical model provided incremental risk stratification. Similar robust associations were observed for fatal coronary heart disease and incident heart failure. EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality and provided incremental prognostic information beyond established clinical and sleep-related factors in this cohort. By integrating respiratory event intensity, cumulative burden, and inter-event interval regularity, EWDB may better characterize cardiovascular stress related to sleep-disordered breathing.

papers.title: The Association of Window Ventilation Frequency with Depressive Symptoms Among Older Chinese People: Perceived Sleep Duration and Psychological Resilience.
papers.abstract: Little is known about the potential mechanism of window ventilation behavior on depressive symptoms in older people. Associations between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms were investigated with modified Poisson regression using the 2018 data of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS), with 11,374 Chinese adults aged 65 years and over. Serial mediation models were applied to investigate if self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience mediated the association between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms. Window ventilation frequency was negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The mitigating effect of high window ventilation frequency on depressive symptoms had the highest efficacy in spring and the lowest in winter. Window ventilation frequency also had a significant link with depressive symptoms through three significant mediating pathways: the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration, the mediating role of psychological resilience, and the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience, separately. Findings of this study highlighted the mechanism that connects window ventilation behavior to depressive symptoms in older adults.

papers.title: Effects of morning versus evening high-intensity exercise on electroencephalographic and autonomic responses in middle-aged women.
papers.abstract: The time of day at which exercise is performed influences physiological responses and performance, and thus its health benefits. This study investigated whether electroencephalographic (EEG) and autonomic nervous system responses to morning versus evening exercise differed in middle-aged women. Thirty women aged 50-60 years were randomly assigned to a morning or evening exercise group. Participants were asked to sleep for seven to eight hours before testing. The morning group exercised at 6:00 am and the evening group at 6:00 pm. EEG-derived indices included the theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) and spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90). Photoplethysmography-derived autonomic indices comprised the HRV index and HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices, measured at rest before and immediately after exercise. Data were analyzed using a two-way mixed-design analysis of variance. For significant interactions, simple effects and change-score analyses were performed. TBR and SEF-90 showed significant group × time interactions, with greater changes from pre- to post-exercise in the morning group. TBR increased and SEF-90 decreased following exercise in both groups, with greater changes in the morning group. The HRV index showed only a significant main effect of time. However, HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices demonstrated significant group × time interactions, with greater autonomic responses in the morning group, as measured by change scores. EEG- and HRV-derived neurophysiological response patterns to high-intensity exercise may vary with exercise timing. Morning high-intensity exercise may elicit greater neurophysiological responses than evening exercise, highlighting the importance of exercise timing in training strategies and recovery.

papers.title: Compositional associations of 24-hour movement behaviors with metabolic syndrome in Korean older adults: a nationwide cross-sectional study using KNHANES 2022-2024.
papers.abstract: Movement behaviors over 24 hours-sleep, sedentary time, and physical activity-are temporally interdependent, but most Korean studies in older adults have analyzed them in isolation. We examined how the 24-hour movement composition relates to metabolic syndrome (MetS) in adults aged ≥ 65 years. We pooled data from the 9th Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES; 2022-2024) and analyzed 4,316 community-dwelling older adults. Daily time in sleep, sedentary behavior, light physical activity (LIPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was rescaled to 1,440 min/day. Isometric log-ratio (ilr) coordinates were entered into weighted logistic regression that accounted for the complex survey design, and 30-min isotemporal substitutions were estimated. Weighted MetS prevalence was 40.4%. Greater relative time in MVPA (ilr1) and LIPA (ilr2) was inversely associated with MetS (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.89-0.96; OR 0.80, 0.70-0.91), whereas a higher sedentary-to-sleep ratio (ilr3) showed a positive association (OR 1.28, 1.02-1.62). Reallocating 30 min from sedentary time to MVPA was associated with about 13% lower predicted odds of MetS (OR 0.87, 0.82-0.93), and even a shift to LIPA showed a small but significant association (OR 0.97, 0.96-0.98). Sex-stratified analyses showed broadly consistent patterns in men and women. In Korean older adults, replacing sedentary time with any form of activity-especially MVPA- was associated with lower predicted odds of MetS, supporting a 24-hour movement perspective for metabolic-health promotion.

papers.title: Not heard or remembered: A daily assessment of experienced intersectional invisibility.
papers.abstract: Intersectional invisibility is the experience of not being remembered, attended to, differentiated, or given credit for contributions, and is most likely to be experienced by people with multiple stigmatized identities. In the present study, we used a smartphone-based longitudinal daily diary design to examine the frequency and downstream consequences of experienced invisibility as they unfold in daily life. Over the course of 10 days, 301 participants reported their daily experiences of invisibility, sleep quality and positive affect, and pre- and post-diary measures of well-being and academic outcomes. As predicted, number of stigmatized identities positively predicted daily experiences of invisibility. For each additional stigmatized identity, the odds of reporting any instance of invisibility on any given day increased by 18%. Daily experienced invisibility was associated with poor outcomes, especially for those with multiple stigmatized identities, including reductions in daily positive affect and sleep quality, and pre- to post-diary decreases in well-being and academic outcomes. There was also evidence of cumulative effects on a short timescale: experienced invisibility from the previous 3 days predicted lower positive affect and worse sleep on the present day. This research suggests invisibility is a chronic experience with negative consequences, experienced by people with multiple stigmatized identities.
papers.journal: The British journal of social psychology

papers.title: A Machine Learning-Based Fall Risk Prediction Model for Middle-Aged and Older Adults with Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease and Arthritis: Development and Geographic Split-Sample Validation.
papers.abstract: Falls impose a major public health burden on middle-aged and older adults. Coexisting cardiovascular disease (CVD) and arthritis further increases fall risk, yet targeted prediction models remain scarce, especially in Chinese populations. We analyzed 633 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study participants aged ≥45 years with comorbid CVD and arthritis at the 2015 baseline. Seven predictors were selected through univariate analysis, LASSO logistic regression (LR), and clinical review. Eight machine-learning algorithms were compared. Among models with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) ≥0.72, the model with the highest specificity was preferred to reduce false-positive referrals. A geographically defined holdout group (n = 110) from different provincial-code regions, but within the same CHARLS source population, was treated as a geographic split-sample rather than independent external validation. Performance was assessed using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1-score, calibration, decision-curve analysis, precision-recall curves, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). During cumulative follow-up, 296 participants (46.8%) reported at least one fall. Random forest (RF) and LR achieved similar internal-validation AUCs (0.730 vs. 0.729); RF was selected because of higher specificity. Internally, RF showed 87.5% specificity, 37.7% sensitivity, 70.3% PPV, 64.2% NPV, and an F1-score of 0.491. Its AUC in the geographic holdout sample was 0.735. Despite similar AUCs, sensitivity and specificity differed substantially between samples, suggesting limited regional stability of the fixed threshold. SHAP identified fall history, ankle pain, activities of daily living impairment, and sleep duration as the most influential predictors. The RF model showed moderate discrimination and a conservative, high-specificity profile. However, its low internal sensitivity means it should not be used alone to rule out falls or as a diagnostic tool. Pending independent validation and regional threshold calibration, it may serve only as adjunctive stratification within a stepped assessment pathway and should not replace routine clinical fall-risk screening.

papers.title: Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic-Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.

papers.title: A machine learning approach to predicting high-risk irritability trajectories across the transition to adolescence.
papers.abstract: Youth irritability, characterized as proneness to anger/frustration, is associated with negative mental health outcomes. This study identified irritability trajectories across the transition to early adolescence and applied machine learning to identify preadolescent predictors of irritability trajectories. Data are from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large longitudinal study that tracks youth development from preadolescence (n = 11,862, ages 8.92-11.08 years, M = 9.91, SD = 0.62). The baseline sample was 47.83% female (n = 5,680), 63.35% White, 15.74% Black, 12.07% Biracial or Multiracial, 2.32% Asian, and 20.30% Hispanic. Using parent-report youth irritability scores across four years, latent class growth analysis (LCGA) identified four distinct irritability trajectories: low stable (n = 8,692, 73.28%), high decreasing (n = 1,083, 9.13%), low increasing (n = 1,449, 12.22%), and high chronic (n = 638, 5.38%). Machine learning approaches generated predictive models for irritability trajectories, including baseline youth psychopathology, physical health, neurocognitive abilities, psychosocial environment, demographics, parent psychopathology, and brain structure metrics. The models demonstrated strong performance in detecting probability of being in the high chronic and low stable trajectories but poorer performance in classifying the irritability trajectories characterized by change. The most prominent predictors included youth externalizing and internalizing problems, parent psychopathology, and sleep problems. Findings provide insight into preadolescent predictors of irritability across a critical developmental period.

papers.title: Analysis of the evolving disease burden of female infertility and its associated risk factors.
papers.abstract: The global burden of female infertility is increasing, yet the roles of metabolic syndrome (MetS) and circadian syndrome (CircS) remain poorly understood. This study aimed to describe the global disease burden of female infertility and examine the associations between MetS, CircS, and infertility. Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data were used to assess trends in infertility prevalence. Cross-sectional data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) were used to evaluate associations between metabolic status and infertility using weighted logistic regression. The global number of women with infertility nearly doubled from 59.8 million in 1990 to 114.5 million in 2023 (ASR, + 25.27%), with the sharpest increase in Western Sub-Saharan Africa (247.6%). Both MetS (OR = 1.41, 95% CI 1.00-1.99) and CircS (OR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.04-2.07) were associated with an elevated risk of infertility. The combined presence of MetS and CircS was also positively associated with infertility (OR = 1.51, 95% CI 1.04-2.18). Among women under 35 years of age, CircS (OR = 1.69; 95% CI 1.00-2.87) and the combination of both syndromes (OR = 1.77; 95% CI 1.02-3.10) were associated with an elevated risk of infertility. Elevated blood pressure was the individual component most strongly associated with infertility. The global burden of female infertility is substantial. Both MetS and CircS are significant risk factors for infertility, with a stronger association for CircS among younger women. Elevated blood pressure showed the strongest association among the individual metabolic components. These findings support integrating metabolic and circadian risk assessment into infertility prevention strategies.
papers.journal: Journal of assisted reproduction and genetics

papers.title: Genetic background modulates MafAS64F-mediated islet ageing in male mice.
papers.abstract: In monogenic diabetes, there is increasing recognition that common polygenic factors can modulate diabetes penetrance beyond the causative mutation(s). A naturally occurring mutation in the gene encoding the essential islet-enriched transcription factor MafA (MafAS64F) produces an unusually long-lived variant protein that predisposes male carriers to MODY. Here we investigated how genetic background modulates disease penetrance in MafaS64F/+ male mice. MafaS64F/+ male mice, either on a mixed genetic background (C57BL/6J and SJL/J) or backcrossed to a C57BL/6J background, were assessed for glucose levels, beta cell function and gene signatures associated with cellular ageing. RNA-seq analysis was performed to identify unique differentially expressed genes (DEGS) and pathways in mixed-background or C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets. These were overlaid on MafA CUT&RUN peaks to identify direct targets that could differentially impact beta cell function in each background. MafaS64F/+ male mice on a mixed background manifested overt diabetes, impaired insulin secretion, accelerated beta cell senescence and dysregulated circadian gene expression, while backcross to C57BL/6J prevented dysglycaemia and maintained insulin secretion in MafaS64F/+ male mice, comparable with control littermates. RNA-seq of C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets revealed relative normalisation of DEGs associated with cellular ageing and circadian regulation. In addition, islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice showed unique downregulation of retinoic acid signalling and cell cycle inhibitor p21, the latter of which modulates cellular ageing and diabetes seen in the mixed-background mouse islets. CUT&RUN mapping revealed that MafA directly impacted expression of (at least) retinoic acid receptor-α (encoded by Rara) in islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice and circadian regulation in islets from mixed-background mice. In sum, these data show that genetic modifiers can impact beta cell regulation of retinoic acid signalling and circadian entrainment to modulate beta cell ageing and disease penetrance in mice modelling MAFA-MODY. Sequencing data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (accession no. GSE299343 for bulk RNA-seq and GSE298664 for CUT&RUN analyses).

papers.title: Human testis-specific TTRP regulates circadian clock as an evolutionarily young natural antisense transcript of PER2.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates a variety of physiological and behavioral processes, endowing the ability to adapt to the cycling environment. Here, we report the identification of TTRP, a TDP-43 pseudogene that emerged in higher Hominoidea species ~8.6 Mya. TTRP is a human testis-specific gene that overlaps with the clock gene PER2 and interferes with PER2 transcription. TTRP encodes a protein that interacts with the clock proteins PER2, BMAL1, and CRY2, and promotes PER2 and CRY1 turnover. The expression of gorilla and bonobo TTRP proteins changes the period and amplitude of circadian rhythms in human cells. Knock-in and expression of human TTRP in mouse testes prolong the brood-interval time and increase the ratio of sperm with high motility. These findings highlight the functional importance of TTRP as a regulator of the circadian clock and suggest that the human circadian clock may be undergoing continuous evolution through the recruitment of novel factors.

papers.title: ERS/ESRS clinical practice guideline for continuous positive airway pressure for the treatment of adult obstructive sleep apnoea.
papers.abstract: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the primary treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), although its effectiveness may vary across OSA subtypes. This joint European Respiratory Society (ERS)/European Sleep Research Society (ESRS) clinical practice guideline evaluates CPAP's impact on patient-centred and prognostically relevant outcomes, comparing it to no or sham treatment in different OSA subgroups. The joint ERS/ESRS Task Force consisted of experts in pulmonology, cardiology and respiratory sleep medicine, patient representatives and methodologists. Questions were formulated using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) framework. A systematic review assessing the effects of CPAP on critical outcomes was performed. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach. Consensus on the direction and strength of the recommendation was informed by Evidence-to-Decision frameworks and achieved through discussions and voting. The Task Force generally suggests CPAP treatment for OSA because of its beneficial effects on sleepiness, other patient-reported outcomes and blood pressure (conditional recommendations). CPAP is recommended in patients with excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) (strong recommendation). Additional specific conditional recommendations are given for patients with moderate-to severe OSA, the elderly, and patients with arterial and treatment-resistant hypertension. The Task Force suggests either CPAP or no treatment in patients without EDS (but taking into account other OSA-related symptoms), in patients with atrial fibrillation with the aim of reducing its recurrence and in patients with impaired glucose metabolism to improve glycaemic control. CPAP is an effective treatment for adults with OSA. However, recommendations for its use vary across different patient subgroups.

papers.title: Hypoxic Burden Is an Important Determinant of Height in Nonobese Children With Sleep-Disordered Breathing.
papers.abstract: The relationship between linear growth and obstructive sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) has not been extensively studied. Hypoxic burden (HB) is a new metric that may better capture end-organ damage in paediatric SDB compared to the traditional apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). This observational cross-sectional study examined the association between HB and linear growth in nonobese children aged 3-9 years with SDB. HB was assessed as the area under the peripheral oxygen desaturation curve, alongside standard polysomnography indices. A cohort of 164 children without comorbidities except for asthma was evaluated for suspected SDB, with demographic and anthropometric data collected. The mean ± standard deviation height z score was -0.05 ± 1.09, and the median [25th; 75th percentile] HB was 1.4 [0.4; 3.5] %min/h. Forty children (24%) had an obstructive AHI greater than 5/h. HB and frequent snoring (≥ 3 nights/week) were significantly and negatively associated with height z score (standardized β = -0.21, p = 0.036 and -0.37, p = 0.043, respectively), whereas AHI did not predict linear growth outcomes. In multivariate analyses, HB remained independently associated with lower height z score and accounted for 7.5% of its variance, compared with 12.7% for ethnicity and 6.4% for body mass index z score. The oxygen desaturation index was also a significant predictor, but it explained less variance in height z score than HB. These findings suggest that intermittent hypoxia may contribute to impaired linear growth in children with SDB, although its contribution is modest and other determinants of growth remain important.

papers.title: Clocks and steroids interaction across the life span.
papers.abstract: The circadian system enables organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes and to align physiology and behaviour with the external light-dark cycle. In mammals, this temporal organisation is coordinated by the central pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which synchronises peripheral clocks through humoral and neural signals throughout the body. The circadian clock and steroid hormones are linked through a reciprocal, multi-level regulatory relationship. While the SCN and peripheral clocks shape the temporal pattern of steroid secretion, steroid hormones feed back onto the SCN and peripheral clocks, thereby modifying clock gene expression, phase, amplitude, synchrony, and network coherence. This interaction is dynamic across the lifespan, as both the clock and the steroid environment change during development, reproductive life, and ageing. During prenatal and early postnatal development, maternal glucocorticoids (GCs) and other perinatal steroid signals provide time-dependent cues that may shape the maturation and long-term function of the circadian system. During reproductive life in females, ovarian steroids dynamically remodel clocks within the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, coordinating reproductive timing with circadian signals from the SCN. In parallel, GCs interact with the reproductive axis and may influence fertility in a time-of-day- and cycle-stage-dependent manner. Disruption of this temporal coordination, for example, by shift work, may impair reproductive and endocrine function. With advancing age, both circadian and endocrine rhythms lose robustness, leading to weakened coordination between the SCN and peripheral clocks, as well as reduced synchrony among cellular clocks within peripheral tissues. These changes contribute to disturbed sleep-wake rhythms, reproductive ageing, and altered stress responsiveness. This review discusses the interaction between steroid hormones and circadian clocks across the life span, highlighting reciprocal regulation as a key mechanism linking temporal organisation to physiology and health.

papers.title: Information avant la lettre: The mathematical constitution of brain waves in early EEG analysis (1929-1932).
papers.abstract: This article examines the epistemological conditions under which the brain's electrophysiological trace was first constituted as a mathematical object of analysis. Rather than treating information as a cultural metaphor externally projected onto the brain, the paper reconstructs how specific tools of signal analysis made the trace into an object that the informational lineage would come to require. Hans Berger's research of 1929-1931 secured the trace as an effect of nervous processes in the brain, but read it as the signal of a single source. The case study is Günther Dietsch's 1932 paper, the first application of Fourier analysis to the EEG signal. The article shows that spectral decomposition did not merely describe the signal but constituted it as a decomposable causal object, resolving a single continuous curve into a discrete set of components, each varying independently of the rest. No improvement of the recording apparatus could achieve this; only the mathematical intervention could. The case is read through the causal-deflationary theory of information in López and Lombardi (2019), according to which a source informs a destination only when a variable of the destination can be manipulated by the source. What 1932 builds is the object of a theory of information needs, not yet the measure that such a theory would later compute on it. That is what avant la lettre means here: mathematics made the trace informational before the theory existed.
papers.journal: Studies in history and philosophy of science

papers.title: Sleep trajectories in pregnancy: associations with trauma exposure, PTSD, and postpartum depression.
papers.abstract: Sleep during the perinatal period is often highly disrupted due to maternal biopsychosocial changes that accompany pregnancy. Poor sleep quality is a symptom of PTSD, while insomnia often emerges after a traumatic event and commonly co-occurs with PTSD. Trauma exposure as well as insomnia have been linked to increased risk for postpartum depression (PPD). The current study examined sleep trajectories across pregnancy and into the postpartum period, the impact of trauma exposure and PTSD on these sleep trajectories, and associations between these sleep trajectories and PPD. Participants completed psychiatric diagnostic evaluations for PTSD and other mental health conditions, as well as validated self-ratings of insomnia and depressive symptoms at four time points across pregnancy and at 6 weeks postpartum. Participants were categorized into one of four groups: (a) trauma exposure with PTSD, (b) trauma exposure with another mental health condition, (c) trauma exposure with no mental health conditions, or (d) no reported trauma exposure or current mental health conditions. Longitudinal growth mixture modeling revealed two distinct sleep trajectories across pregnancy: poor sleep (28.5%) and normative sleep (71.5%). Trauma-exposed participants with PTSD or other mental health conditions were more likely to have poor sleep profiles. Participants with poor sleep profiles had significantly higher depressive symptoms. These findings support the need for targeted interventions addressing insomnia in trauma-exposed pregnant women with psychiatric sequelae to improve outcomes during and after pregnancy.

papers.title: Effects of nighttime graduated compression tights on overnight changes in lower-limb circumference in healthy young women with subjective leg swelling: A randomized crossover trial.
papers.abstract: BackgroundTransient lower-limb swelling may occur in healthy young women during daily life. This study examined whether wearing graduated compression tights during sleep enhanced overnight reductions in lower-limb circumference and affected subjective sleep quality or morning fatigue.MethodsIn this randomized, open-label, two-period crossover trial, female university students aged 18-28 years with subjective lower-limb swelling were assigned 1:1 to compression-first or no-compression-first sequences. Each 14-day period was separated by a 7-day washout. With compression, participants wore graduated compression tights during sleep after daytime acclimation. Co-primary outcomes were between-condition differences in overnight circumference change at the ankle, calf, and thigh. Secondary outcomes were subjective sleep quality and morning fatigue. Self-reported morning leg swelling was assessed at each time point. Mixed-effects models were used, with Holm adjustment for three primary outcomes.ResultsForty-six participants were randomized and 44 completed both periods. Compared with no compression, compression resulted in greater overnight reductions at the ankle (least squares mean difference, -0.23 cm; 95% confidence interval, -0.33 to -0.13; adjusted p = 0.0001), calf (-0.35 cm; -0.52 to -0.18; adjusted p = 0.0004), and thigh (-0.28 cm; -0.47 to -0.08; adjusted p = 0.0066). Perceived morning leg swelling was less likely with compression (30.6% vs. 58.4%). The OSA-MA sleep-length factor was lower at Time3 (nominal p = 0.03), but no other sleep-related outcome or morning fatigue differed significantly. No adverse events were reported.ConclusionsWearing graduated compression tights during sleep enhanced overnight reductions in lower-limb circumference. Although the differences were modest (approximately 2-4 mm) and their clinical importance remains uncertain, the accompanying reduction in perceived morning swelling suggests that these changes may have perceptible relevance to participants. Nighttime compression may facilitate the overnight reduction of transient lower-limb swelling under everyday living conditions.

papers.title: Developing a Theory-Based Sleep Hygiene Education Intervention for Adults with Insomnia: An Intervention Mapping and Content Validation Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep hygiene education (SHE) is commonly used in insomnia management, yet its observed effectiveness is modest, potentially reflecting limitations in its implementation, including simplified content, limited standardization, and suboptimal delivery formats. This study aimed to systematically develop a theory-based SHE program for adults with insomnia. The SHE intervention was developed following Phase I of the Medical Research Council framework and operationalized using Steps 1-4 of intervention mapping. Stakeholders, including 10 experts and 10 individuals with insomnia, were engaged throughout development to review and validate the program content, enhance its acceptability, and ensure its appropriateness. The resulting theory-based SHE program comprises two integrated components: (1) an educational module addressing insomnia knowledge, evidence-based sleep hygiene behaviors, and self-regulatory strategies for initiating and sustaining practice; and (2) brief follow-up telephone consultations designed to reinforce adherence and support implementation planning. Experts and individuals with insomnia endorsed the program's overall appropriateness, with minor refinements suggested for specific elements. This study presents a structured development and content validation of a theory-driven SHE program informed by behavioral science, empirical evidence, and stakeholder input. The intervention targets key limitations of traditional SHE approaches and provides a strong foundation for future feasibility testing.

papers.title: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor-Associated Bruxism: Neuropharmacologic Mechanisms and Clinical Implications.
papers.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)-associated bruxism is an increasingly recognized medication-associated phenomenon, although its incidence, neuropharmacologic mechanisms, and optimal management remain incompletely understood. This focused narrative review examines the clinical evidence, proposed mechanisms, and therapeutic implications of SSRI-associated bruxism. Available literature demonstrates recurring temporal associations between SSRI initiation or dose escalation and the emergence of jaw clenching, tooth grinding, pain, and related orofacial symptoms across multiple agents. Proposed mechanisms are multifactorial and may involve altered monoaminergic regulation within central motor networks, including serotonergic-dopaminergic interactions, 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) receptor 1A (5-HT1A) signaling, and possible noradrenergic contributions; however, these mechanisms remain unconfirmed in affected patients. Adjunctive buspirone is the most consistently described pharmacologic strategy and may permit the continuation of an otherwise effective SSRI, although evidence for benefit remains primarily case-based. The literature is limited by heterogeneous bruxism definitions, inconsistent differentiation between awake and sleep manifestations, variable antidepressant exposures, and sparse objective physiologic assessment. Prospective studies using standardized assessment methods and controlled treatment designs are needed to clarify incidence, susceptibility, pathophysiology, and treatment response.

papers.title: The Use of Montelukast in Pediatric Asthma and Anti-Inflammatory Effects - Easy Choice or a Balancing Act?
papers.abstract: Montelukast is a selective cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 antagonist with an established, though nuanced, role in the management of asthma and allergic rhinitis. By inhibiting leukotriene-mediated signaling, montelukast targets a pathway involved in bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular permeability, eosinophil recruitment, cytokine release, and airway remodeling. Available evidence indicates that montelukast may reduce several markers of allergic inflammation, including fractional exhaled nitric oxide, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, eosinophil-derived mediators, adhesion molecules, selected cytokines, and markers related to airway remodeling. These effects are most consistently demonstrated in asthma and allergic rhinitis, while evidence in chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis, and other inflammatory conditions remains limited or exploratory. Montelukast's once-daily oral administration and age-adjusted pediatric formulations make it a practical option in selected children, particularly when inhaled therapy is difficult or adherence is problematic. However, montelukast should not be regarded as a direct substitute for corticosteroid-based anti-inflammatory therapy. Current evidence and guideline positioning support its use mainly as an add-on controller, or an alternative when more efficacious treatment is contraindicated. The benefit-risk balance is further shaped by concerns regarding neuropsychiatric adverse events, especially in children, although evidence remains heterogeneous. Current data show no increased risk of severe, diagnostically coded neuropsychiatric events, yet milder sleep-related and behavioral symptoms are consistently reported, so that caution and active monitoring remain warranted. Overall, montelukast remains a biologically plausible and clinically useful therapy, but its value depends on appropriate patient selection and realistic expectations of its anti-inflammatory potential.

papers.title: Neonatal Pain Assessment After Night Shifts in NICU Professionals: A Within-Subject Exploratory Eye-Tracking Study.
papers.abstract: Night-shift work may influence attention and emotion processing, potentially affecting clinical assessment. We investigated whether neonatal pain evaluation and associated visual-attentional and pupillary responses differed between rested and post-night-shift assessments in experienced NICU professionals. In this prospective within-subject study, 20 NICU professionals evaluated 42 standardized video clips of term neonates exposed to nonnoxious, short noxious, or prolonged noxious stimuli. Participants were assessed after at least 1 day off work and within 2 h after completing one or more consecutive night shifts. Pain ratings, eye-tracking metrics, and pupil diameter were compared between conditions. Overall pain ratings did not differ significantly between rested and post-night-shift assessments (3.56 ± 0.69 vs. 3.61 ± 0.72; p = 0.643; Cohen's d = 0.11). Pupillary responses also showed no statistically significant differences. Exploratory eye-tracking analyses suggested reduced visual exploration after night-shift exposure, including fewer visits across several areas of interest and shorter fixation duration on the infant's body. These secondary analyses were unadjusted for multiple comparisons and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating. No statistically significant differences in neonatal pain ratings or pupillary responses were detected following routine night-shift work, whereas exploratory eye-tracking measures suggested differences in visual-attentional patterns. Given the small, selected sample and exploratory design, these findings do not establish equivalent or preserved performance between conditions. Larger prospective studies incorporating objective sleep measures and clinically relevant outcomes are warranted.

papers.title: Perioperative Anesthetic Considerations for Temporal Bone Tumor Resection in Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23)-Related Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) are uncommon, predominantly benign neoplasms frequently associated with dysregulated phosphate metabolism through the overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Elevated levels of FGF23 lead to phosphate depletion, which may impair tissue oxygen delivery, central respiratory drive, and respiratory muscle function. Systemic manifestations may include osteomalacia and neuromuscular dysfunction, with an increased risk of respiratory and cardiovascular complications. PMTs often present with nonspecific clinical findings and may remain unrecognized during the perioperative period, presenting significant challenges for anesthetic planning and management. We report the case of a 72-year-old male with tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO), a right temporal mass, and multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea. The patient reported progressive headaches and general weakness. After neurosurgical evaluation, he underwent elective surgical excision under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, he developed hypotension following induction of anesthesia, requiring vasopressor support with ephedrine boluses and a continuous phenylephrine infusion. The remainder of the procedure was uneventful, and the patient was extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of recognizing potential complications in patients with metabolic abnormalities presenting with PMTs, particularly disturbances in phosphate homeostasis that may have significant anesthetic implications. The use of video laryngoscopy, judicious administration of neuromuscular blocking agents, and an individualized anesthetic strategy facilitated secure airway management, minimized cervical manipulation, and supported an uneventful recovery. Moreover, integrating anesthetic selection with comprehensive perioperative planning is essential to address the metabolic, musculoskeletal, respiratory, and hemodynamic challenges associated with TIO, particularly in patients with significant comorbidities.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Evidence to Clinical Translation: A Narrative Review of Chinese Herbal Medicine for Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders and a major public health problem worldwide. Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is widely used as a complementary and alternative approach for chronic insomnia. Clinical studies have reported preliminary evidence of benefit for Chinese herbal formulas, whereas mechanistic research has examined single herbs, extracts, active constituents, and compound formulas using multi-omics analysis, network pharmacology, molecular prediction, and experimental validation. However, clinical studies are typically small and of inconsistent methodological quality, with limited long-term follow-up, while mechanistic evidence remains fragmented and lacks systematic integration and translational validation. These limitations restrict the development of CHM interventions from experimental evidence to clinically testable interventions for insomnia. This narrative review evaluates existing research across five translational dimensions, namely chemical characterization and preparation quality, exposure and pharmacodynamic evidence, mechanism and target validation, sleep-related clinical endpoints, and safety. It aims to clarify the current state of research on CHM interventions for insomnia and to identify key limitations and priorities for future research. Most available evidence comes from preclinical studies, which suggest that CHM may influence sleep-related processes through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and serotonergic signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis-autophagy balance, and the brain-gut-microbiota axis. Much of this evidence reflects changes in biochemical markers or pathway activity, while only a few studies directly test target function. Clinical studies provide preliminary evidence of short-term improvements in subjective sleep outcomes. However, clinical translation remains limited by insufficient evidence for objective sleep improvement and long-term efficacy and safety. Future work should carry a few well-characterized interventions through the full evidence chain, prioritizing standardized preparations, exposure and pharmacodynamic assessment, objective sleep endpoints, long-term follow-up, and safety.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing and Sleep Fragmentation in Relation to Atrial Fibrillation Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most prevalent cardiac arrhythmias worldwide. This study aimed to evaluate the association between sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), primarily assessed using the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and AF risk, with additional analysis of sleep fragmentation parameters such as wake after sleep onset (WASO) and arousal index (AI). This systematic review and meta-analysis followed Cochrane Handbook recommendations and PRISMA guidelines, with protocol registration in PROSPERO (No. 127490). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational cohort studies assessing sleep disturbances and AF were included. MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from inception to February 2026. Extracted data included study characteristics, demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and sleep metrics. Outcomes were incident and recurrent AF. A random-effects model was applied. Twenty-one cohort studies (611,898 participants) were included. SDB was associated with increased incident AF risk (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.41-1.97; I 2 = 66.5%), with consistent Bayesian estimates. A dose-response relationship showed a 2% increase in AF risk per unit rise in AHI. For AF recurrence, 11 studies (n = 1810) demonstrated a significant association (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40-1.72; I 2 = 0%), supported by Bayesian analysis. Sleep disturbances are significantly associated with both incident and recurrent AF and may represent modifiable risk factors.

papers.title: Step-by-Step Protocol for Fluorescence-Based Analysis of Uptake in Transporter-Expressing Xenopus laevis Oocytes.
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis oocytes are widely used as a heterologous expression system for investigating the function of membrane proteins due to robust expression of heterologous protein and a low endogenous transport background. Traditionally, transporter activity in oocytes has been assessed using electrophysiology or radiolabeled uptake assays, approaches that are constrained by the requirement for electrogenicity of the transport process, availability of radiolabeled compounds, and instrumentation. Here, we describe a fluorescence-based uptake assay that enables direct and rapid quantification of transporter activity using a fluorescence plate reader. The protocol uses the Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose transporter 1 (SUC1) and its fluorescent substrate esculin as a case for how to set up the assay. The workflow includes optimizing assay conditions, sample preparation, fluorescent measurements, and downstream data analysis using R. This method can readily be adapted to other transporter-substrate pairs, and it supports applications such as transporter inhibitor screening, mutational analysis, characterization of kinetic properties, or indirect substrate specificity testing through competition assays. Overall, this protocol provides a simple and scalable alternative to traditional techniques, eliminating the need for radiolabeled compounds or electrophysiology while enabling easy quantitative assessment of transporter activity. Key features • Provides a simple, plate reader-based fluorescence uptake assay for quantifying transporter activity in Xenopus laevis oocytes. • Adaptable to any transporter with a compatible fluorescent substrate, supporting rapid testing of substrate specificity indirectly through competition assays or mutant screening. • Includes a complete workflow from assay setup and conduction to data analysis, suitable for both initial characterization and routine functional testing of membrane transporters.

papers.title: Association of Burning Mouth Symptoms with Sleep Quality, Stress and Xerostomia in Middle-Aged and Elderly Patients - a Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a long term syndrome of oral pains that is prevalent among the middle aged and the aged people. It is usually associated with poorly understood symptoms, including sleeping difficulties, psychological stress and xerostomia (dry mouth). The objective of the systematic review was to establish the association between the burning mouth symptoms and sleep quality, stress and xerostomia, through a systematic review of the literature at hand. A thorough electronic database search was carried out leading to the identification of 10 eligible studies, according to a set of inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results showed that BMS is closely linked with low sleep quality, high levels of psychological distress and perceived dry mouth, which may lead to a multifactorial interaction, which determines the extent of symptoms and the quality of life of patients. This research paper is added to the scientific literature as it summarizes existing evidence and emphasizes the need to thoroughly assess and treat patients with BMS using multidisciplinary approaches.

papers.title: Intermittent hypoxia interventions for inducing ventilatory acclimatization to high altitude?
papers.abstract: Accumulation of ∼200 h of hypoxia exposure (pre-acclimatization) has been suggested to prevent the development of acute mountain sickness when a person is subsequently exposed to high altitude. These pre-exposures are typically undertaken intermittently at or near the place of residence, primarily during sleep in hypoxic tents, and are likely to induce effective ventilatory acclimatization. However, the physiological consequences of different modes of intermittent hypoxia (IH) exposure on ventilatory acclimatization remain largely obscure and are the subject of much controversy. The aim of this review is therefore to summarize and discuss the findings of relevant studies and draw on our long-term practical experience to address the effects of IH exposure on ventilatory acclimatization and to provide suggestions for effective pre-acclimatization. We provide a balanced overview of studies investigating the effects of different types of altitude/hypoxia exposure on the hypoxic ventilatory response and renal compensation to hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis. Although it has been demonstrated convincingly that the hypoxic ventilatory response can increase by 50%-100% with only a few short IH sessions (1 h per day for 7 days), the available data on the effects of IH on renal compensation do not permit definitive conclusions to be drawn. Long-term exposure to IH over several weeks appears to induce renal compensation effectively, allowing for a full ventilatory response and favourable oxygenation at high altitude. To clarify definitively which strategies are most suitable, long-term systematic investigations of various IH strategies are urgently needed.
